title: Relief or displacement? How teachers are negotiating generative AI’s role in their professional practice
venue: ACM Conference proceedings (venue not otherwise specified in text)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers are responding to the introduction of generative AI (genAI) in their professional practice, with attention to the tensions between perceived relief and perceived displacement. Rather than studying student outcomes or testing a specific instructional intervention, the authors ask how teachers perceive genAI, what opportunities and challenges arise when districts introduce it, and how teachers negotiate its use within professional, pedagogical, and ethical boundaries.

The study is based on semi-structured interviews with 22 teachers from a large U.S. school district that was an early adopter of genAI and had encouraged use of MagicSchool AI and other tools. Participants taught across elementary, middle, and high school levels and across subject areas including STEM, social studies, special education, CLDE, literacy, and media/CTE. Interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by the Teacher Response Model, focusing on teachers’ value-driven decisions, contextual constraints, and perceptions of what was possible with genAI.

The paper finds that teachers were neither simply adopting nor rejecting genAI. Instead, they described adoption as motivated by district encouragement, peer validation, burnout prevention, and creative instructional possibilities, while reluctance stemmed from lack of time, stigma around “cheating,” preference for established routines, and environmental concerns. Teachers also described carefully setting boundaries around AI use to preserve professional judgment, ensure factual accuracy, protect student data, and regulate student exposure. The authors conclude that sustainable genAI integration depends less on the tool itself than on district policy clarity, teacher-led professional development, ethical guidance, and support for students’ critical AI literacy.

identified_tools.name: MagicSchool AI
identified_tools.description: A teacher-facing generative AI platform for creating instructional materials, lesson supports, feedback, and related classroom/administrative content.
identified_tools.use_case: The district encouraged teachers to integrate MagicSchool AI into their classrooms, and participants described using it for lesson planning, creating materials, feedback, and other instructional tasks.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI generative AI chatbot for open-ended text generation, drafting, editing, and conversational assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers reported using ChatGPT for lesson planning, grading support, communication drafting, feedback drafting, and general teaching assistance.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s generative AI chatbot/model family used for open-ended text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers reported using Gemini for lesson and assessment support, feedback-related tasks, and general instructional planning.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic’s generative AI chatbot/model family for text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: A few participants reported using Claude among their broader set of genAI tools for professional tasks.

identified_tools.name: Canva
identified_tools.description: A design and content-creation platform with AI-assisted features used for generating visual and instructional materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers reported using Canva alongside genAI tools for creating classroom and professional content.

identified_tools.name: TalkingPoints
identified_tools.description: A communication platform used to support multilingual family engagement and messaging, with AI-assisted features reported in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers reported using TalkingPoints in their professional practice, including communication-related tasks.

identified_tools.name: Diffit
identified_tools.description: A teacher tool for adapting and differentiating instructional content and reading materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers reported using Diffit to adapt materials for students and generate differentiated supports.

identified_tools.name: Brisk Learning
identified_tools.description: An education tool used to support instructional and classroom tasks, including AI-assisted content generation and feedback-related workflows.
identified_tools.use_case: A participant reported using Brisk Learning as part of their genAI toolset.

identified_tools.name: Adobe AI
identified_tools.description: Adobe’s AI-assisted creative tools used for generating or editing digital content.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers reported using Adobe AI for professional and instructional content creation tasks.

identified_tools.name: EduAid
identified_tools.description: An education-related AI tool mentioned by participants as part of their instructional toolset.
identified_tools.use_case: A participant reported using EduAid among multiple genAI tools.

identified_tools.name: HeyGen
identified_tools.description: An AI avatar/video generation tool used to create narrated or presented video content.
identified_tools.use_case: A teacher used HeyGen to create micro-PDs and planned to use it for substitute-delivered lessons.

identified_tools.name: Read Along
identified_tools.description: A reading-support tool used to assist literacy practice and language-related learning.
identified_tools.use_case: A participant listed Read Along among tools used in their professional practice.

identified_tools.use_case: Teachers reported using Pear Deck as part of their classroom technology toolkit.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools or chatbots used for drafting, feedback, lesson planning, communication, and other text-based support when no single named product is being isolated.
identified_tools.use_case: This is a qualitative study of how teachers navigate genAI in practice; many participants used multiple tools, and the paper’s findings are about genAI use broadly rather than a controlled evaluation of one system.

findings.finding_summary: In interviews with 22 teachers, genAI was commonly perceived as saving time on routine professional tasks such as lesson planning, drafting communications, grading support, and creating materials. Teachers framed these efficiency gains as helping reduce burnout and cognitive load, although the study did not quantify effects.
findings.measure: Perceived time saving, burnout prevention, and workload reduction in semi-structured interviews

findings.finding_summary: Teachers described district endorsement, professional learning opportunities, and peer validation as important drivers of uptake, while unclear policies, stigma, privacy concerns, and lack of training constrained use. The paper suggests adoption is shaped by institutional context rather than tool capability alone.
findings.measure: Perceived institutional supports and constraints from interview themes

findings.finding_summary: Teachers used genAI to broaden instructional approaches, but they also stressed boundaries to preserve professional judgment, trust, and student learning. The paper reports descriptive patterns only; it does not test subgroup effects by experience, subject, grade band, school context, or deployment format.
findings.measure: Descriptive interview themes on instructional use, boundaries, and sustainability

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study, not a controlled efficacy design. It provides rich descriptive evidence about teachers’ perceptions and contexts, but it cannot estimate causal effects or subgroup moderation.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful perceived benefits and constraints, especially around time savings and institutional support, but there are no quantified effect sizes or experimental impacts. The practical influence is descriptive and context-specific rather than demonstrated as a measurable intervention effect.
